newsitem.title: UK: Shaken sterling crawls off low by late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Shaken sterling crawls off low by late Europe.

text.p: Sterling inched off its low at the end of a session in which it plunged more than three and a half pfennigs on Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies' reported remark expressing concern about sterling's strength.
It also recouped some of its losses against the dollar after it fell to a five-month low early in the day.

"Looking at the levels, we've probably come down as much as you'd expect for now... I would expect a small bounce from here, although longer-term I still think we'll see 2.69 (for sterling/mark)," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London.

"Cable also got into oversold territory after the fall this morning. So I would look for a bit of a pullback... although I think that if you get a bounce, people could sell into that," Beauchamp said.

Sterling was at 2.7115/25 marks at 1550 GMT, down from its early high of 2.7482 and its late Tuesday level of 2.7355/65. Cable was at $1.5935/40 after touching a five-month low of $1.5889, and was down from its late Tuesday level of $1.6050/60.
The pound was hit early in the day when Japan's Jiji news agency quoted Davies as saying the pound was slightly overvalued against the mark.
Last week sterling rose to 2.7733 marks, its highest level since it fell out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.

The pound got little solace from a clarification of Davies' comment. A spokesman for the British embassy in Tokyo, where Davies had been addressing a Japanese banking industry group, said the comment referred to the view of financial markets and not that of the central bank.
"Looking at the forward rate for the pound, it seems the market is indicating the pound's future value would level out or drop against the mark," the spokesman quoted Davies as saying.

Sterling/mark was not affected by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer's comment that Germany still wanted a stable mark and that he was not interested in a foreign exchange correction that went beyond fundamentals.

Analysts and traders did not see sterling's plunge today as the start of a new trend in the currency, saying sterling/mark had been due for a downward correction and that cable had been heading lower today in any case.

"Cable seems to be gravitating towards $1.5800, a level people seem to be looking at, and the (Davies) comment seemed to be an excuse to take it down there," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW.
"We've been very overbought (in sterling/mark) and the market is due for a bit of a pullback in the long-term uptrend, and that's what we're seeing now," Cooperative Bank's Beauchamp said.
